{
  "hook": "Sitting at over 900 meters in elevation, this specific site stands out from the rest of the Sierra de Gredos because it is planted on schist rather than the region's ubiquitous granite. That geological shift, combined with a co-planting of Garnacha and the red-fleshed Alicante Henri Bouschet, produces a darker, more brooding expression of mountain wine. It trades the typical ethereal floral notes of the region for deep, firmly structured dark fruit.",
  "wine_summary": "Comando G fundamentally changed how the wine trade views Spanish Garnacha by treating the high-altitude, abandoned vineyards of the Sierra de Gredos like grand cru Burgundy. Founders Daniel Landi and Fernando Garcia focus on old, bush-trained vines clinging to steep slopes, working them biodynamically to coax out site-specific transparency. While their portfolio is famous for pale, highly aromatic reds, El Reventon breaks that mold entirely.\n\nThe inclusion of Alicante Henri Bouschet—a teinturier grape with naturally pigmented flesh—darkens the color and fortifies the tannic spine of the wine. Combined with the punishing mountain sun and low-yielding old vines, the resulting blend balances intense concentration with the high-toned herbal lift characteristic of the Cebreros appellation. It delivers serious weight, hitting 15% ABV in warm vintages like 2020, yet carries that alcohol with surprising agility due to the site's natural acidity.",
  "terroir_expression": "The Sierra de Gredos is defined by its severe continental climate and high-altitude radiation, which forces vines to develop thick skins and deep roots just to survive. While the broader Cebreros appellation is famous for degraded sandy granite, the El Reventon vineyard sits on a rare vein of schist and slate. This darker, heat-retaining rock absorbs the intense daytime sun and radiates it back at night, ripening the Alicante Bouschet fully while imparting a distinct smoky, iron-like minerality to the finish. That schist soil directly translates to firmer, more angular tannins in the glass compared to the powdery grip of granite-grown Garnacha.",
  "vinification_summary": "To manage the inherent power of this site, the winemaking relies heavily on whole-cluster fermentation—a technique where intact grape bunches, stems included, go into the vat to add structural tension and spicy aromatics while slightly lowering the perceived alcohol. Following a gentle maceration with minimal punch-downs to avoid extracting harsh seed tannins from the Alicante Bouschet, the wine ages for 14 months in large, neutral oak vessels. These oversized foudres allow for slow micro-oxygenation, softening the blend's rustic edges without masking the vineyard's distinct mineral signature beneath new wood flavors.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Braised oxtail with star anise: The intense reduction of the sauce matches the wine's dark fruit concentration, while the star anise picks up the stemmy, whole-cluster spice.",
    "Smoked beef brisket (Texas style): The heavy bark and rendered fat desperately need the wine’s firm tannins and high alcohol to cleanse the palate, and the wine's schist-driven smokiness echoes the pit fire.",
    "Morcilla (blood sausage) stuffed piquillo peppers: A classic regional match where the iron-rich, earthy sausage aligns perfectly with the rustic, savory depth of the Alicante Bouschet.",
    "Wood-fired portobello mushrooms with thyme: For a plant-based option, the intense umami and woodsmoke mimic meat, giving the wine's structural tannins plenty of protein-like compounds to bind with."
  ],
  "comparable_wines": [
    "Domaine de Trévallon (Provence) — Shares the same dark, brooding intensity and wild, scrubby herbal notes, driven by a rugged southern climate and intense sun.",
    "Clos Mogador (Priorat) — Offers a similarly powerful, schist-grown Garnacha blend that balances high alcohol with intense mineral drive and firm structure.",
    "Envínate Lousas 'Viñas de Aldea' (Ribeira Sacra) — Though lighter in body, it shares the wild, whole-cluster stem spice and slate-driven tension found in El Reventon."
  ],
  "style_profile": "Garnacha and Alicante Bouschet blend offering full-bodied weight, firm tannins, and a smoky, schist-driven mineral core",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Keep this in the cellar for at least five years past the vintage date to let the firm tannins and high alcohol integrate. It has the structural density to evolve beautifully over 15 to 20 years in a temperature-controlled environment.",
  "value_assessment": "At roughly $90 to $120 a bottle, this sits squarely in the premium tier of modern Spanish wine. It competes directly with high-end Priorat like Terroir al Límit or single-vineyard bottlings from Descendientes de J. Palacios in Bierzo. It justifies the price tag through its extreme rarity and its unique position as the darkest, most structured wine in the highly coveted Comando G lineup.",
  "market_position": "Collectors of new-wave Spanish wine aggressively hunt down allocations of this cuvée upon release. You will almost exclusively find it on the reserve lists of Michelin-starred Spanish restaurants or in the cellars of serious terroir geeks. It is not a casual Tuesday night pour, but rather a benchmark bottle for those tracking the revival of historic mountain vineyards.",
  "insider_take": "Do not open this expecting the pale, Pinot Noir-like fragility that Comando G is famous for in their other bottlings. The addition of Alicante Bouschet and the shift to schist soils make this a bruiser in its youth, demanding serious decanter time or a decade in the cellar. If you want immediate, floral gratification from the Gredos, buy their La Bruja de Rozas instead; buy El Reventon only if you have the patience to wait for it.",

parsed.hook: Sitting at over 900 meters in elevation, this specific site stands out from the rest of the Sierra de Gredos because it is planted on schist rather than the region's ubiquitous granite. That geological shift, combined with a co-planting of Garnacha and the red-fleshed Alicante Henri Bouschet, produces a darker, more brooding expression of mountain wine. It trades the typical ethereal floral notes of the region for deep, firmly structured dark fruit.
parsed.wine_summary:
Comando G fundamentally changed how the wine trade views Spanish Garnacha by treating the high-altitude, abandoned vineyards of the Sierra de Gredos like grand cru Burgundy. Founders Daniel Landi and Fernando Garcia focus on old, bush-trained vines clinging to steep slopes, working them biodynamically to coax out site-specific transparency. While their portfolio is famous for pale, highly aromatic reds, El Reventon breaks that mold entirely.

The inclusion of Alicante Henri Bouschet—a teinturier grape with naturally pigmented flesh—darkens the color and fortifies the tannic spine of the wine. Combined with the punishing mountain sun and low-yielding old vines, the resulting blend balances intense concentration with the high-toned herbal lift characteristic of the Cebreros appellation. It delivers serious weight, hitting 15% ABV in warm vintages like 2020, yet carries that alcohol with surprising agility due to the site's natural acidity.
parsed.terroir_expression: The Sierra de Gredos is defined by its severe continental climate and high-altitude radiation, which forces vines to develop thick skins and deep roots just to survive. While the broader Cebreros appellation is famous for degraded sandy granite, the El Reventon vineyard sits on a rare vein of schist and slate. This darker, heat-retaining rock absorbs the intense daytime sun and radiates it back at night, ripening the Alicante Bouschet fully while imparting a distinct smoky, iron-like minerality to the finish. That schist soil directly translates to firmer, more angular tannins in the glass compared to the powdery grip of granite-grown Garnacha.
parsed.vinification_summary: To manage the inherent power of this site, the winemaking relies heavily on whole-cluster fermentation—a technique where intact grape bunches, stems included, go into the vat to add structural tension and spicy aromatics while slightly lowering the perceived alcohol. Following a gentle maceration with minimal punch-downs to avoid extracting harsh seed tannins from the Alicante Bouschet, the wine ages for 14 months in large, neutral oak vessels. These oversized foudres allow for slow micro-oxygenation, softening the blend's rustic edges without masking the vineyard's distinct mineral signature beneath new wood flavors.
food_pairing: Braised oxtail with star anise: The intense reduction of the sauce matches the wine's dark fruit concentration, while the star anise picks up the stemmy, whole-cluster spice.

Smoked beef brisket (Texas style): The heavy bark and rendered fat desperately need the wine’s firm tannins and high alcohol to cleanse the palate, and the wine's schist-driven smokiness echoes the pit fire.
Morcilla (blood sausage) stuffed piquillo peppers: A classic regional match where the iron-rich, earthy sausage aligns perfectly with the rustic, savory depth of the Alicante Bouschet.
Wood-fired portobello mushrooms with thyme: For a plant-based option, the intense umami and woodsmoke mimic meat, giving the wine's structural tannins plenty of protein-like compounds to bind with.
comparable_wines: Domaine de Trévallon (Provence) — Shares the same dark, brooding intensity and wild, scrubby herbal notes, driven by a rugged southern climate and intense sun.
Clos Mogador (Priorat) — Offers a similarly powerful, schist-grown Garnacha blend that balances high alcohol with intense mineral drive and firm structure.
Envínate Lousas 'Viñas de Aldea' (Ribeira Sacra) — Though lighter in body, it shares the wild, whole-cluster stem spice and slate-driven tension found in El Reventon.
parsed.style_profile: Garnacha and Alicante Bouschet blend offering full-bodied weight, firm tannins, and a smoky, schist-driven mineral core
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Keep this in the cellar for at least five years past the vintage date to let the firm tannins and high alcohol integrate. It has the structural density to evolve beautifully over 15 to 20 years in a temperature-controlled environment.
parsed.value_assessment: At roughly $90 to $120 a bottle, this sits squarely in the premium tier of modern Spanish wine. It competes directly with high-end Priorat like Terroir al Límit or single-vineyard bottlings from Descendientes de J. Palacios in Bierzo. It justifies the price tag through its extreme rarity and its unique position as the darkest, most structured wine in the highly coveted Comando G lineup.
parsed.market_position: Collectors of new-wave Spanish wine aggressively hunt down allocations of this cuvée upon release. You will almost exclusively find it on the reserve lists of Michelin-starred Spanish restaurants or in the cellars of serious terroir geeks. It is not a casual Tuesday night pour, but rather a benchmark bottle for those tracking the revival of historic mountain vineyards.
parsed.insider_take: Do not open this expecting the pale, Pinot Noir-like fragility that Comando G is famous for in their other bottlings. The addition of Alicante Bouschet and the shift to schist soils make this a bruiser in its youth, demanding serious decanter time or a decade in the cellar. If you want immediate, floral gratification from the Gredos, buy their La Bruja de Rozas instead; buy El Reventon only if you have the patience to wait for it.
